https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/03/second-ch.body: Uzbekistan “Second Chance”: Nationwide project transforming lives of convicts in Uzbekistan Uzbekistan's Second Chance project is providing English language and vocational training to 311 young inmates across 11 penal institutions, with 88.6% successfully completing the English A1 curriculum and 79.5% achieving computer literacy proficiency, as authorities plan to expand the privately funded rehabilitation and employment initiative nationwide by 2027. Today, 12:00 4 min read 765 views 0 comments 0 More than 300 inmates aged 18–30 across 11 penal institutions in Uzbekistan are receiving English language instruction and vocational training under the nationwide Second Chance ( Ikkinchi Imkon ) project, with initial assessments showing that 88.6% of participants successfully completed the English A1 curriculum and 79.5% achieved proficiency in computer literacy. The initiative, launched on June 1, 2026, aims to prepare young inmates for employment after their release and support their reintegration into society through language education, digital skills and vocational training. The Second Chance project began operating in the Tashkent, Navoi and Kashkadarya regions on June 1, 2026. A total of 311 inmates were selected to participate following testing and oral interviews. The participants subsequently began intensive English language and computer literacy courses. Final assessments conducted during the first five months of the project showed that 88.6% of participants had successfully mastered the English A1 curriculum, while 79.5% demonstrated proficiency in computer literacy. The highest regional results were recorded in Kashkadarya and Navoi. In Kashkadarya, the successful completion rate reached 96.6% for English and 98.3% for computer literacy. In Navoi, the corresponding figures were 98.9% and 87.5%, respectively. Two penal institutions recorded a 100% success rate in both subjects: Colony No. 5 in Qiziltepa and Colony No. 3 in Qarshi. To ensure independent evaluation, participants' knowledge is assessed by external specialists rather than the instructors conducting the courses. Testing is carried out monthly through a dedicated digital platform. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced the Second Chance initiative during a meeting with young people at the Koʻksaroy residence on February 24, 2026. The project was subsequently formalized through Presidential Resolution No. PQ–117, adopted on March 27, 2026. Its main objectives are to support the employment of individuals released from penal institutions, facilitate their reintegration into society and reduce the risk of repeat offenses. The initiative was initially introduced in three regions as a pilot project. According to the project plans, it will be extended to all penal institutions across Uzbekistan by 2027. The Second Chance project targets inmates aged 18–30 who are serving sentences for the first time. Participation is restricted to individuals whose offenses are not classified as especially grave and who do not pose a significant threat to society. Individuals convicted of crimes involving information technology are not eligible to participate. Training is organized through intensive programs lasting between eight and twelve months. The curriculum includes English language instruction from A1 to B2 level, with language courses lasting 12 months. Participants can also study computer literacy, computer servicing and network technologies, soft skills, data analysis and entrepreneurship through online marketplaces. Upon successful completion of the relevant training program, participants receive a nationally recognized electronic qualification certificate in their chosen profession or field. The project is fully financed by UNICON-SOFT LLC and does not require funding from the state budget. The company covers organizational and material expenses, including instructors' salaries, classroom equipment, teaching materials and supplies for participants. Classrooms are equipped with computers, electronic whiteboards and educational furniture. UNICON-SOFT also provides learning materials, notebooks, pens and other supplies required for the courses. On August 29, 2026, memoranda of cooperation were signed between the Penitentiary Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, UNICON-SOFT LLC, Vatan University, MAAB Innovation and SZS Trucking. Under the cooperation arrangements, Vatan University proposed providing a full scholarship to the most successful graduate of the project each year. The scholarship would cover four years of tuition. MAAB Innovation, identified as Microsoft's first official partner in Uzbekistan, expressed its intention to provide free data analysis training to participants with computer literacy skills and a good command of English. SZS Trucking proposed offering short-term training courses to graduates proficient in English, with the possibility of subsequent employment at the company. The Second Chance initiative is scheduled to expand from its initial pilot regions to penal institutions throughout Uzbekistan by 2027. The project combines language instruction, digital education, vocational training and cooperation with private employers to support participants' transition into employment following their release. The initiative also provides for employment opportunities for graduates who successfully complete the required training and acquire the necessary qualifications. Блок YouTube В его автомобиле милиционеры обнаружили сверток с белым порошкообразным веществом. Еще один сверток нашли в предполагаемом месте закладки. Дома у задержанного находились оборудование для выращивания растений, жидкости в различных емкостях, упаковочные материалы и весы. Правоохранители изъяли подготовленные к продаже марихуану, гашиш и героин. По предварительным расчетам, стоимость изъятых веществ при реализации могла составить 4,5 миллиона сомов. В телефонах подозреваемого нашли Telegram-профиль интернет-магазина «А» и другие аккаунты, предположительно связанные с приобретением крупных партий наркотиков, психотропных веществ и семян марихуаны. По информации МВД, задержанный является одним из организаторов интернет-магазина, через который наркотики распространяли в Бишкеке и Чуйской области.

https://www.hudson.org/human-rights/us-n.body: SVG Reports Oct 30, 2026 Hudson Institute US National Security and Antisemitism, Issue 2 | The October 7 Mobilization, Militant Convergence in Europe, Iran’s Campaign in Britain, and the Flydubai Attack Michael Doran Senior Fellow and Director, Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East Ludovic Hood Senior Fellow, Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East Zineb Riboua Research Fellow, Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East Natalie Arbatman Research Associate, Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East Michael Doran , Ludovic Hood , Zineb Riboua & Natalie Arbatman Reports Caption Pro-Palestine protesters gather during a demonstration outside Downing Street on October 26, 2026 in London, United Kingdom. (Getty Images) This report, the second edition of a new series from Hudson Institute’s Center on Peace and Security in the Middle East, tracks how antisemitic and anti-Zionist ideas travel across platforms, languages, countries, and political movements—and how foreign adversaries weaponize these ideas against the United States and its allies. Issue 1 demonstrated how a Chinese-led axis, which includes Russia and Iran, uses antisemitism and anti-Zionism to shape the political environment in which US policymakers operate and to persuade Americans that their country’s alliances are burdens. [1] This issue shows this same logic at play in four different dynamics: the organization of transnational protests, the fusion of European far-left militancy with pro-Palestinian extremism, Iranian intelligence operations directed at US allies, and the radicalization of individuals whose paths to violence run through the schools, airlines, and security systems of several US partners. Monthly Monitor | October 2026 The third anniversary of the attacks of October 7 offered a rare view of how maleficent actors are manipulating the forces of antisemitism and anti-Zionism against US interests. Over the course of several weeks, these forces operated at protest marches in Washington, DC, near air bases in the United Kingdom, and in the skies over Saudi Arabia—and in every case, they turned hostility toward Israel into costs for the United States and its partners. In the UK, British counterterrorism police arrested two men under suspicion of aiding Iranian intelligence in connection with a suspected plot against US aircraft at Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford in Gloucestershire, England. Designed to occur near the anniversary of the attacks of October 7, the plots in Britain included a coordinating alliance in London, a far-left protest network, and funding from Shanghai-based US tech mogul Neville Roy Singham. Chinese and Iranian state media amplified these efforts. In Germany, meanwhile, intelligence services concluded that domestic and diaspora extremist networks are targeting the country’s defense industry. And in the Middle East, a pilot employed by Flydubai and radicalized in Melbourne, Australia, by takfiri ideology—a jihadist doctrine that justifies violence against those it deems unbelievers—targeted an aircraft carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Israel. These activities prompt the question, Why does hostility toward Israel travel so easily from one arena to another? This report argues that anti-Israel sentiments offer a common enemy to movements and governments that otherwise share few interests. Anti-imperialist militants in Berlin, Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) organizers in New York, Islamist networks in Melbourne, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in Tehran emerged from different milieus. But Israel gives these actors a common cause and, increasingly, common targets in their war against the West. The United States, as Israel’s principal ally and the guarantor of the order these actors oppose, is already in their sights. This issue examines four recent instances in which these anti-US forces have weaponized anti-Israel sentiment against the United States and its partners. The first part explores how a centralized anti-West alliance planned the worldwide Global Day of Action protests on October 10, 2026. The second part describes how German intelligence services discovered how hostility toward Israel unites Islamist, far-left, and pro-Palestinian extremists in Germany, and how the United States and its European allies treat the same networks under different laws. The third part examines Iran’s covert campaign in the United Kingdom, where operatives from the Islamic Republic conducted surveillance of Jewish and Israeli sites and masterminded an alleged plot against the RAF base that houses US strategic bombers. The final part traces the Flydubai attacker’s path of radicalization from Melbourne to the cockpit, and shows how his attack exposed weak vetting and security screening processes that Tehran moved quickly to exploit. 1. The October 7 Anniversary: A Coordinated Global Mobilization Image 1. Anti-Israel Protest in New York on October 7, 2026 Source: Getty Images. What Happened On October 10, 2026, activists in dozens of countries staged what they described as a Global Day of Action under the banner “End the Genocide, Defend the Land.” [2] The Global Alliance for Palestine (GAFP), a coalition launched in London in July 2025, planned and convened the campaign, which it billed as an “open, decentralised platform.” [3] The group produced an interactive map that listed 322 events over three days, and 179 organizations signed on to participate in the day of protests. [4] The alliance’s steering committee, according to a GAFP press release, includes many well-known members of the European and international left: Jeremy Corbyn, the former leader of the UK Labour Party; Yanis Varoufakis, the former finance minister of Greece; Gerry Adams, the former president of Sinn Féin; Palestinian politician Mustafa Barghouti; and former South African politician Ronnie Kasrils. [5] The coordination required for organizing these protests rested on a common playbook. The organizers’ own materials show how they devised their anti-Israel campaign. First, the alliance standardized its message. Organizers provided a single toolkit to every local organization that included the same posters in seven languages, ready-made handheld placards and so-called street demands, a common set of slogans and hashtags, and prepared social-media kits. These tools enabled hundreds of rallies on several continents to speak with one voice. [6] A GAFP concept paper set the tone of the protests, calling for messaging that was “disciplined, credible, urgent and impossible to ignore.” [7] Second, the alliance instructed its chapters to engage in disruption. The toolkit recommended “peaceful blockades,” walkouts, banner drops, and “die-ins,” and urged participants to “shut down city squares, encircle government buildings, and blockade complicit corporate hubs.” [8] The toolkit also offered guidance on “legal, stewarding, and participant support,” and prepared local organizers for confrontations with police and the courts. [9] Third, organizers moved to apply pressure from the street to the legislative body. The group’s toolkit included template letters to lawmakers. [10] In September, the alliance’s secretary-general, Anas Altikriti, announced a dedicated legislative track for the campaign. “Public pressure must cross the threshold of legislative assemblies,” he said. [11] Although the GAFP is based in London, the United States became the principal theater of the group’s actions. Israel’s Ministry of Diaspora Affairs counted 262 planned GAFP events across 37 countries in the days before the anniversary of October 7. The United States accounted for 45 of these, more than any other country. [12] A later tally from the Ministry of Diaspora Affairs recorded 357 demonstrations worldwide between October 1 and October 14. [13] American participants in these events included groups from a network already drawing scrutiny from the US government. Neville Roy Singh

https://www.azernews.az/region/266730.ht.body: Turkish journalist criticizes attempts to strain ties with Azerbaijan 3 November 2026 15:13 (UTC+04:00) Akbar Novruz Read more Turkish journalist Yılmaz Özdil has criticised attempts to create tensions between Türkiye and Azerbaijan over the Palestinian issue, arguing that foreign policy should be guided by national interests rather than religious considerations. Speaking in a video published on YouTube, Özdil pointed to the contrasting regional partnerships of Iran and Israel, noting that Tehran maintains close relations with Armenia while Israel has developed a strategic partnership with Azerbaijan. According to the journalist, these relationships demonstrate that national interests and strategic considerations, rather than religious affiliations, determine the foreign policies of individual states. Özdil criticised certain political and public circles in Türkiye for focusing on Azerbaijan's relations with Israel and attempting to influence Baku's domestic and foreign policy decisions. "It is not the right approach for Türkiye to experience friction in its relations with Azerbaijan over the issue of Palestine. On October 29, on Türkiye's Republic Day, the President of Palestine visited the Greek Cypriot side, the Republic of Cyprus. Yet, for the sake of these Palestinians, we risk straining our ties with Azerbaijan. Israel was one of the first states to recognize Azerbaijan after it declared independence in 1991, whereas Palestine has, for many years, supported Armenia’s position. Azerbaijan has not forgotten Palestine’s stance regarding Armenia," he stated. The journalist also recalled Türkiye's previous concerns regarding Palestinian relations with the PKK and the Armenian militant organisation ASALA, arguing that Ankara had subsequently set aside those disagreements. Turning to Azerbaijan's military cooperation with Israel, Özdil emphasised that the relationship had developed over many years and had played a role in strengthening Azerbaijan's defence capabilities. "Azerbaijan acquired a significant portion of the weapons it used during the Second Karabakh War from Israel. While Türkiye frequently highlights its own provision of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to Azerbaijan, it should be noted that Azerbaijan has been collaborating with Israel on the joint production of UAVs since 2009," he said. Özdil also addressed the historical foundations of Azerbaijan–Türkiye relations, referring to Azerbaijan's decision to commemorate Victory Day on November 8 rather than November 10, the date on which the trilateral statement ending the 2020 war was signed. He described the choice of November 8 as a gesture of respect for Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder of the Republic of Türkiye, whose death is commemorated annually on November 10. "This decision demonstrates the depth of the fraternal ties between the two nations. During Türkiye’s War of Independence in 1919–1920, the Azerbaijani people not only provided material aid to Türkiye but also participated in the national resistance movement, sacrificing their own lives. All of this shows that the Azerbaijan-Türkiye brotherhood is rooted in a strong historical foundation," Özdil emphasised. Tags: Journalists Azerbaijan-Turkiye

https://www.azernews.az/nation/266716.ht.body: Sabina Aliyeva re-elected as Azerbaijan’s Human Rights Commissioner for seven-year term 3 November 2026 12:47 (UTC+04:00) Qabil Ashirov Read more Sabina Aliyeva has been re-elected as Azerbaijan’s Human Rights Commissioner (Ombudsperson) for a new seven-year term. The relevant decision was adopted during a plenary session of the Milli Majlis (Azerbaijan’s parliament) on Monday. Three candidates were nominated for the position: Sabina Aliyeva, Elshana Valiyeva and Jeyhun Garajayev. Aliyeva secured the highest number of votes and was elected for a seven-year term. Of the MPs who participated in the vote, 100 supported her re-election, one voted against and seven abstained. Following her re-election, Aliyeva took the oath of office before parliament. She pledged to perform her duties with honour and dignity, uphold the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Azerbaijan, and carry out her responsibilities independently and impartially. Aliyeva also expressed gratitude to President Ilham Aliyev, the Speaker of the Milli Majlis and members of parliament for the confidence placed in her. Aliyeva was first elected Azerbaijan’s Human Rights Commissioner on November 29, 2019, from among three candidates nominated by the President of Azerbaijan. Professional background Sabina Aliyeva Yashar gizi was born on May 7, 1980, in Baku. She graduated with honours from Baku Secondary School No. 8 in 1996. Between 1996 and 2000, she studied at the Faculty of Law of Baku State University, completing her bachelor's degree with honours. She subsequently obtained a master's degree in law from the same university between 2000 and 2002, also graduating with distinction. From 2009 to 2012, Aliyeva pursued additional higher education in international relations at the Academy of Public Administration under the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan. In 2016, she defended her dissertation on the application of international legal standards concerning the protection of the rights of persons with disabilities in Azerbaijani legislation, earning a PhD in Law. Aliyeva began her professional career at the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Azerbaijan in 2000. After holding various positions at the institution, she was appointed Deputy Head of the Constitutional Court's Administration in 2015. In 2016, she was awarded the third-degree rank of State Councillor. On November 29, 2019, the Milli Majlis elected her Human Rights Commissioner of Azerbaijan, a position she has held since then. Her principal responsibilities as Ombudsperson include protecting human and civil rights, investigating alleged violations of rights and freedoms, monitoring compliance with human rights standards by government authorities, and promoting legal awareness. In her international activities, Aliyeva was elected Vice-President of the Asian Ombudsman Association in 2023. That same year, she became a member of the Board of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation's Ombudsman Association. She also serves as a mentor for the Yüksəliş competition, established by the President of Azerbaijan, and was a member of the Organising Committee for COP29. Ombudsperson election procedure and eligibility requirements Under Azerbaijani legislation, the Human Rights Commissioner is elected for a seven-year term, and the same person may hold the position for a maximum of two terms. Thirty days before the incumbent's term expires, the President submits three candidates to the Milli Majlis for consideration. Parliament must adopt a decision on the election of a new Ombudsperson within 15 days. The Ombudsperson is prohibited from engaging in political activities or belonging to any political party. The officeholder also cannot serve in the management of a non-governmental organisation. Any activities incompatible with the position must be terminated within five working days of election. On the day of election, the Ombudsperson takes an oath before the Milli Majlis, pledging to uphold the Constitution and laws, discharge official responsibilities with honour and dignity, and act independently and impartially. A candidate must be an Azerbaijani citizen aged at least 30, hold a higher education degree, have professional experience in human rights protection and demonstrate high moral standards. Individuals holding dual citizenship, having obligations to another state, or serving in the legislative, executive or judicial branches of government are ineligible. The restriction also applies to individuals engaged in other paid employment, with the exception of scientific, educational and creative activities, as well as those declared legally incapacitated by a court or convicted of serious or particularly serious crimes. https://tass.com/politics/2212059.body: Russia’s mission lambasts UNESCO report on journalists’ safety The mission specified that a significant number of journalists who have been killed, as officially reported by the Russian side, is lacking from the lists attached to the report © AP Photo/ Thomas Padilla PARIS, November 2. /TASS/. UNESCO has once again ignored Russia’s data on journalists’ deaths in its regular report on the safety of journalists, having betrayed its own values, the Russian mission to this organization said. "We regret to note that the Secretary General’s report prepared by the Secretariat to the Intergovernmental Council of the International Program for the Development of Communication (IPDC) has once again failed to uphold UNESCO’s values. Once again, a significant number of journalists who have been killed, as officially reported by the Russian side, is lacking from the lists attached to the report. These journalists have also been excluded from the statistics cited in the report," the mission said. Russian diplomats pointed to the flaws in the methodology used to select information cited by the organization’s secretariat while compiling the report and emphasized that the number of killed journalists, according to UNESCO’s allegedly "verified" data, is many times lower than the actual figure. They also called on UNESCO Director General Khaled El-Enany to condemn the killing of every journalist, to "correct the mistakes of the organization’s previous leadership, instruct the secretariat to review the methodology in collaboration with member states" and adopt the changes at the next IPDC session in 2028. "There is no statute of limitations for crimes against journalists. Journalists killed during armed conflicts are civilians. Their murders will entail all the legal consequences associated with this status. Russia will spare no effort to ensure that all killed journalists are properly accounted for in UNESCO’s statistics and that their murders are duly condemned," the Russia mission said in a statement. Earlier, UNESCO issued the Report on the Safety of Journalists and the Danger of Impunity, where it said that 189 journalists were killed from the beginning of 2024 to late 2025. As many as 127 of them were killed in zones of combat operations. According to the report, 40% of these deaths were caused by drone attacks. The bulk of the fatalities were reported in Palestine (62), Mexico (17), and Sudan (14). The conflict in Ukraine, according to the UNESCO statistics, claimed the lives of 12 reporters during this period. https://daryo.uz/en/2026/11/02/president.body: Uzbekistan President calls for recognition of Uzbek citizens’ work experience abroad President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has called for recognizing Uzbek citizens’ work experience abroad when calculating pensions, expanding bilateral agreements on pension rights, and improving employment opportunities for returning migrants, with 250,000 returnees targeted for job placement by the end of 2026. Yesterday, 16:05 2 min read 2 176 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Farrux Aliyev President Shavkat Mirziyoyev addressed the recognition of employment history and pension rights of Uzbek citizens working abroad during a meeting on November 2. The president noted that Uzbek citizens are legally employed in more than 40 countries, where they pay taxes and pension contributions. However, their periods of employment abroad are not taken into account when they return to Uzbekistan. "Their work experience abroad must be recognized upon their return to the homeland—it is essential that this be factored in, especially when it comes to calculating pensions," the president stated. During the meeting, it was reported that Uzbekistan had signed bilateral agreements on the recognition of employment history and pension rights with Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan and Turkey this year. However, similar agreements have not been concluded with other countries. The president emphasized the need to establish such agreements with countries where large numbers of Uzbek citizens are employed, including Germany, Russia, Japan, South Korea and countries in the Baltic and Balkan regions. Officials were instructed to conduct negotiations with their foreign counterparts and report on concrete results by the end of the year. The meeting also addressed employment opportunities for citizens returning to Uzbekistan after working abroad. Since the beginning of the year, 1,116,000 people have returned from abroad. Among them are specialists who gained experience in industry, construction, logistics, services and agriculture while working in Germany, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Japan and Russia. Source: Presidential Press Service Mirziyoyev noted that these specialists had worked at major industrial enterprises abroad and acquired knowledge of modern technologies and professional work practices. Regional governors and sector heads were instructed to offer them suitable employment and make use of their knowledge and experience. A platform will be developed to record the employment history, professions and work experience of citizens who have returned from abroad. The platform will be integrated into a system accessible to regional governors and sector heads. A target has been set to find suitable employment for 250,000 returnees by the end of the year. Citizens wishing to pursue entrepreneurship will also receive guidance and the necessary conditions for starting their activities. During the meeting, it was announced that citizens who encounter problems while working abroad will be able to request assistance through the "Online Mahalla" platform. A unified migration center will also be established in every region of Uzbekistan. Starting next year, responsibility for sending citizens abroad for employment will be fully transferred to the most reliable private-sector recruitment agencies. Under the new arrangement, recruitment agencies will receive an incentive payment of UZS 1.5mn (over $120) for each person they successfully place in a high-income job. # Citizen Reintegration Programs # Employment Promotion Initiatives # International Labor Agreements # President Shavkat Mirziyoyev # Unified Migration Centers # Uzbekistan Labor Policy Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? Photo: Presidential press service Its architecture will combine traditional local styles with modern design solutions. The project is intended to bring together Bukhara’s cultural and gastronomic heritage with contemporary tourism services in one location. Construction of engineering and utility networks is currently underway across a 10-hectare section of the site, with around 50 pieces of heavy machinery involved. Photo: Presidential press service According to project estimates, the center will create 2,000 jobs and attract an additional 2 million tourists to Bukhara annually. It is also expected to generate up to UZS 288 billion in revenue for the local budget. Mirziyoyev instructed officials to create an environment worthy of Bukhara’s reputation and present the city’s rich heritage to the world more widely. He stressed that local residents should benefit from new employment opportunities and income generated by tourism. Photo: Presidential press service Officials were tasked with implementing the project in line with these objectives. During the visit, the president also received briefings on preparations for Bukhara’s infrastructure ahead of summits scheduled to take place in 2027 and issued further instructions.

https://en.kabar.kg/news/presidential-el.body: Kabar Agency Kabar Presidential elections in Kyrgyzstan will take place on January 27, 2027. To ensure the successful conduct of this political campaign, the Central Election Commission (CEC) has begun preparatory work. A series of measures is underway, including equipping polling stations with necessary gear and accepting applications from candidates. Kabar agency spoke with Aidana Zhupueva, head of the department for the organization of electoral process at CEC, regarding preparations for the upcoming presidential elections. — How are preparations for the upcoming presidential elections progressing? How many polling stations will be open across the country? — There are 2,492 polling stations in Kyrgyzstan. Regarding the establishment of polling stations abroad, we recently held discussions with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. At present, based on proposals from the ministry, plans are in place to open approximately 100 polling stations abroad, spanning 94 cities across 35 countries. In the past, additional polling stations were also set up in shopping centers and marketplaces. For the presidential elections, polling stations for remote voting will also be established. Furthermore, as you may know, polling stations for remote voting were utilized during the previous parliamentary elections. We are currently working with local authorities and territorial election commissions to analyze areas with the highest population density. Based on this, polling stations for remote voting will also be opened within Kyrgyzstan. As of today, we have a sufficient supply of electoral equipment. Prior to the elections, all equipment will undergo testing and verification. The Republican Headquarters has been established for the elections. The headquarters is headed by the Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers, Adylbek Kasymaliev, with the CEC Chairman Tynchtyk Shainazarov, serving as co-chair. The Republican Headquarters meeting took place on October 6, and a second meeting is also planned. Our primary focus is equipping the territorial election commissions. It is crucial that power supply and heating meet established requirements; to this end, we are coordinating with local government authorities. Additionally, we are providing stationery and informational signage to be displayed outside the polling stations. These materials have already been delivered to Osh and Manas cities. Currently, all territorial election commissions are fully staffed; their chairpersons and secretaries are establishing schedules and organizing duty shifts. — How many personnel are involved across the 2,492 polling stations? — There are 56 territorial election commissions nationwide, comprising 672 members. The 2,492 precinct election commissions have a total membership of 25,000. — How many applications have been received from candidates so far? — At present, three candidates have submitted documents to CEC, expressing their intent to run for the presidency. Presidential elections differ from elections for the Jogorku Kenesh (parliament). In previous parliamentary elections, participating parties and independent candidates would first submit an application, open an election fund, and only then pay an electoral deposit. This deposit is not returned to the candidate; instead, it is transferred to the state budget. Now, those wishing to run for president must submit their application and pay the electoral deposit simultaneously. The current electoral deposit is 1 million soms. A candidate must choose one of the designated banks, either "Abank" or "Eldik Bank" to open an account and establish an election fund. From the funds in this account, the candidate must transfer the required amount to the Central Election Commission. We must be provided with a document confirming this payment; without it, we cannot accept any other documentation. Consequently, a candidate must first submit proof of payment of the electoral deposit, followed by their formal application. Furthermore, a presidential candidate is required to collect between 30,000 and 60,000 signatures from voters. In previous presidential elections, the signature-collection process was conducted on paper; it is now carried out in an electronic format. The "Tunduk" mobile application features a dedicated section for elections. Upon initiating a request to provide a signature, a signature form appears, displaying a list of candidates along with their photographs. Each voter may support their chosen candidate by providing their signature. A voter may submit their support for a given candidate only once. A common question is whether a signature can be withdrawn if it was provided for a candidate by mistake once support for a candidate has been registered, it cannot be retracted. This is a key distinction in the current process. To be eligible as a candidate for the presidency, an individual must be a citizen of Kyrgyzstan and have reached the age of 35 by the election day, must have resided in the country for a total of at least 15 years, and must be proficient in Kyrgyz language. Furthermore, a candidate must have no criminal record, must have ceased any religious activity within the last five years, and must not be affiliated with any criminal groups. These are the requirements. — When will the signature-collection process begin? — We will stop accepting applications from prospective candidates at midnight on November 12. Following this, the signature-collection process will take place, concluding at midnight on December 7. Subsequently, CEC will spend 10 days verifying the signature-collection documentation. Candidate registration will close at midnight on December 20. Registered candidates may begin their campaign activities on December 23. Campaigning must cease at 8:00 a.m. on January 26, 2027. January 26 will be a "day of silence"; on this day, citizens who are unable to visit a polling station, due to health issues or other reasons may cast their votes elsewhere. Such individuals must submit an application to their local precinct election commission two days prior to election day. — Have there been any instances where election campaigning began earlier than permitted by law? What measures have been taken? — Recently, posts have circulated on social media, some by bloggers urging support for specific individuals running as candidates (e.g., "This person is running as a candidate; let’s support them"). The CEC has a working group dedicated to monitoring campaign activities, and they have issued warnings in these instances. — How much funding will be spent on the presidential election? — According to the budget approved by the Central Election Commission, 1.2 billion soms will be allocated for the presidential election. Of this amount, 240 million soms is earmarked for the possibility of a repeat vote. A total of 53 million soms has been allocated for equipping and supplying polling stations abroad, as well as for other related tasks. — Will gifts be presented to citizens voting for the first time? — Starting November 23, members of the Central Election Commission will hold meetings with students from higher education institutions and vocational schools across the country. Out of a total of 4.3 million registered voters, 42% are young people. During these meetings, the importance of youth participation in elections will be explained, along with details on how the electoral process works and the conditions the Central Election Commission has put in place for voters. Additionally, the Central Election Commission operates a Civic Education Center, which also collaborates with youth departments within municipal administrations. As for those who have just turned 18, no gifts will be presented to them. — How many international observers are expected for the presidential election? — Immediately after the election date was set, we sent letters to the central election commissions of other countries and to various international organizations. https://kz.kursiv.media/en/2026-11-03/en.body: Photo: primeminister.kz, photo editor: Dastan Shanay Kazakhstan and China plan to establish a joint direct investment fund with up to $200 million in capital. The announcement came after a meeting between Kazakhstan’s Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin and China’s Minister of Finance Lan Fo’an . The two officials held talks on the sidelines of the 2nd Tien Shan Forum for Central Asia Economic Cooperation. According to the Kazakhstani government’s press service, Kazakhstan first proposed the initiative at a high-level meeting in Shanghai in July to support the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR). The proposal sets the fund’s initial target size at up to $200 million, with the possibility of further expansion. To speed up the fund’s launch, Zhumangarin also proposed identifying financial institutions from both countries that would develop a common approach to its operations. «For practical steps toward financing our projects, we need to build a comprehensive Kazakh-Chinese financial architecture. We are currently developing several complementary mechanisms, each designed to address specific objectives,» he said. These mechanisms include the Kazakh Invest Fund, involving Silk Road Finance Corporation; a Kazakh-Chinese private equity fund involving the national holding company Baiterek and the Silk Road Fund; and financing mechanisms supported by Baiterek, the Development Bank of Kazakhstan, China Development Bank, China EximBank, Bank of China, ICBC and Sinosure, among others. «I propose consolidating existing and emerging mechanisms through a unified Kazakh-Chinese ‘window’ for project financing and insurance, without the need to establish a new organization. This would enable the creation of a comprehensive financial package for each priority project encompassing long-term lending, insurance coverage, guarantees, financing in Chinese yuan, and, where necessary, equity participation,» Zhumangarin said. To test the proposed mechanism, the two sides will select several pilot projects and support them at every stage, from the initial investment decision to financial close. This process will help identify and remove systemic barriers that currently delay major investment projects. The two sides also discussed expanding cooperation with China’s Exim Bank to finance priority infrastructure projects. Kazakhstan is currently working on several strategically important initiatives to develop its transport and utility infrastructure. Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has relieved Nurlan Sauranbayev of his post as Minister of Transport, according to a presidential decree. Prior to his ministerial tenure, Sauranbayev held extensive leadership roles across Kazakhstan's public and corporate sectors, notably leading national railway operator Kazakhstan Temir Zholy and serving in key defense and energy positions. Sauranbayev was born on May 20, 1967. He began his career as General Director of Enbek (1991-1997), before serving as Executive Director of the Congress of Entrepreneurs of Kazakhstan (1997-1998). From 1998 to 2000, he headed the Passenger Transportation Directorate of the Kazakhstan Temir Zholy state enterprise. He then served as First Vice President of ANPZ OJSC (2000-2002) and Director of the Engineering and Service Services Department at KazMunayGas National Company JSC (2002-2004). In 2004-2007, Sauranbayev was General Director of TenizService LLP. From July 2007 to June 2010, he held the positions of Managing Director for Oil Transportation and Managing Director for Service Projects at KazMunayGas. On May 18, 2011, he was appointed Vice Minister of Industry and New Technologies of Kazakhstan, serving until August 25, 2014. From August 2014 to October 2016, he served as Deputy Minister of Defense. In 2017, Sauranbayev headed the organizing committee of the headquarters responsible for preparations for and the holding of the EXPO 2017 International Specialized Exhibition. In November 2017, he was appointed mayor of Shymkent, serving until June 2018. From January 2019 to April 2021, he headed the Department of State Control and Organizational and Territorial Work at the Presidential Administration of Kazakhstan. On April 9, 2021, Sauranbayev became Chairman of the Management Board of Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), a position he held until June 30, 2025. On June 30, 2025, he was appointed Minister of Transport of Kazakhstan and was reappointed to the post on September 3, 2026. https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/4242257..body: Home Azerbaijan Azerbaijani Parliament approves Sabina Aliyeva’s re-election as Ombudsperson Azerbaijan Document 3 November 2026 12:34 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Office of the Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsman) of the Republic of Azerbaijan Alish Abdulla Parliamentary Correspondent Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 3. During today’s plenary session, members of the Azerbaijani Parliament approved the re-election of Sabina Aliyeva as the country's Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsperson), according to a Trend' s correspondent present at the meeting. Three candidates were nominated for the position of Ombudsperson: Sabina Aliyeva, Elshana Valiyeva, and Jeyhun Garajayev. Following the vote, Sabina Aliyeva secured the highest number of votes and was elected Ombudsperson for a seven-year term. Sabina Aliyeva, who has been re-elected as the Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsperson) of Azerbaijan, took the oath of office in the parliament. In the parliament, Sabina Aliyeva swore to perform her duties with honor and dignity, to abide by the Constitution and laws of Azerbaijan, and to act independently and impartially. Aliyeva expressed her gratitude to the President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, the Speaker of the Parliament, and the MPs for the trust placed in her. Sabina Aliyeva was first elected Ombudsperson by the Azerbaijani Parliament on November 29, 2019, from among three candidates proposed by the President of Azerbaijan. Sabina Aliyeva was born on May 7, 1980, in Baku. In 1996, she graduated from Baku Secondary School No. 8 with a certificate of distinction. She pursued her bachelor’s degree (1996–2000) and master’s degree (2000–2002) at the Faculty of Law of Baku State University, graduating with honors at both levels. Between 2009 and 2012, she pursued additional higher education in International Relations at the Academy of Public Administration under the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan. In 2016, she earned a PhD in Law after defending her dissertation on the application of international legal norms, specifically regarding the protection of the rights of persons with disabilities, within the framework of Azerbaijani legislation. She began her professional career in 2000 at the Constitutional Court of Azerbaijan. Following service in various roles, she was appointed Deputy Chief of the Staff of the Constitutional Court in 2015. In 2016, she was awarded the rank of 3rd-class State Counselor. On November 29, 2019, she was elected by the Azerbaijani Parliament as the Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsperson) of Azerbaijan, a position she has held ever since. As Ombudsperson, her primary areas of activity include the protection of human and civil rights, the investigation of instances where rights and freedoms have been violated, the monitoring of state bodies to ensure compliance with human rights, and the promotion of legal awareness. As part of international activities, in 2023, the Ombudsman was elected Vice-President of the Asian Ombudsman Association. That same year, the Ombudsman was elected as a member of the Board of Directors of the Ombudsman Association of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation. Furthermore, the Ombudsperson serves as a mentor for the "Yukselish" competition, established by the President of Azerbaijan, and was a member of the COP29 Organizing Committee. The Ombudsman may not engage in political activities nor be a member of any political party. Additionally, the Ombudsperson may not hold a leadership position within a non-governmental organization. Within five business days of being elected to the post, the Ombudsperson must cease any activities incompatible with their status. On the day of their election, the Ombudsperson takes an oath at a session of the Azerbaijani Parliament, pledging to abide by the Constitution and the laws, to perform their duties with honor and dignity, and to act independently and impartially. A citizen of Azerbaijan may be elected as Ombudsperson, provided they are at least 30 years of age, hold a higher education degree, possess experience in the field of human rights protection, and demonstrate high moral standards. Individuals who hold dual citizenship, have obligations toward other states, serve within the legislative, executive, or judicial branches, engage in other paid activities (excluding scientific, pedagogical, or creative work), have been declared legally incompetent by a court, or have been convicted of serious or especially serious crimes are ineligible for this position. Particular attention was paid to regional cooperation, including the outcomes of the October events held in Turkmenistan’s Awaza National Tourist Zone. “President Serdar Berdimuhamedov noted the constructive nature of the meeting held within the framework of this visit,” the press release stated, referring to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s participation in the CIS Heads of State Council meeting and the Caspian Environmental Summit in Awaza in October. Araghchi, in turn, highlighted the importance of the events held in Awaza, noting that their results had made a significant contribution to advancing regional cooperation. The sides also discussed trade and economic ties, with Berdimuhamedov describing Iran as one of Turkmenistan’s important trade and economic partners. The meeting concluded with both sides expressing confidence in the further development of friendly and good-neighborly relations across areas of mutual interest. Listen to this article 6 min This audio is automated Learn more Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country would cease strikes on Russian oil refineries -- as demanded by US President Donald Trump -- if the United States quickly provides Kyiv with Patriot air defense missiles. Zelenskyy, in an interview with Fox News on November 1, said he had conducted "different and several" discussions with the US president and his aides on the matter. "We [said] we can't not respond after Russia's attack on our energy, after Russia is killing our people, attacks on our electricity, gas, refineries, on everything," he told host Trey Yingst . SEE ALSO: Moscow Reports Drone Attack On Nizhny Novgorod As Russian Strikes Cut Power In Ukraine "We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative: Give us Patriot missiles. We will find money; [it's] not just aid.... We will pay for it." Zelensky said if Washington provided the missile systems for one month, Ukraine would cease attacks on Russian refineries for the same amount of time. Could Take 'Several Years' The US State Department on October 30 announced the approval of a critically needed sale of Patriot air defense interceptors to Ukraine worth $2.1 billion to strengthen Kyiv's defenses against increasing Russian aerial attacks. Zelenskyy, however, has warned that it could take "several years" for the 500 missile interceptors to arrive. Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post that "500 PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number" and could form an effective defense package this winter, but he added that "deliveries may begin only in a few years." "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors," the Ukrainian president said. The evacuation of residents followed a localized cease-fire between Ukraine and Russia brokered by US first lady Melania Trump. Dozens of buses carrying civilians left the war-torn town of Oleshky for the first time in more than four years on October 30, with people choosing whether to travel to Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory. Its residents were effectively trapped, with no way to escape the area, surrounded by land mines and cut off from the outside world. "We managed to escape from this hell," an evacuee named Liubov (not pictured) told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service as buses arrived in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region on October 31. Once home to around 24,000 people, Oleshky's population dwindled to fewer than 2,000 since the full-scale war began in February 2022. https://www.rferl.org/a/iran-europe-targ.body: Iran Is Europe In Iran's Crosshairs? Tehran Hints At Wider Military Reach By Kian Sharifi November 02, 2026 14:20 CET Is Europe In Iran's Crosshairs? Tehran Hints At Wider Military Reach Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Bunting of Iranian flags flies next to a missile on display during the 47th anniversary of the Islamic Revolution in Tehran on February 11. Iran and the United States have traded threats for weeks even as they pursue diplomacy, with the possibility of military escalation after the US midterm elections still looming. A statement attributed to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on October 31 directed the armed forces to be ready to respond to an attack "immediately, effectively, and with no geographical restriction." That last point has fueled speculation in Iran about what it could entail and whether Tehran has the capability to deliver on its threat. When the United States and Israel first attacked Iran on February 28, Tehran responded by striking military and civilian sites in Arab states across the Persian Gulf, insisting it was targeting US interests in the region. Analysts say the Islamic republic hoped that regionalizing the conflict and striking the territory of US allies would pressure Washington into halting its attacks. SEE ALSO: Iran's Long-Distance Strikes On Diego Garcia Put Europe On High Alert Some in Tehran now suggest the next phase of the war -- if it reignites as Trump has threatened -- would go further. Conservative lawmaker and former Foreign Minister Manuchehr Mottaki said the next conflict "will not be a regional war." Speaking on state television after Khamenei's statement was released, Mottaki touted Iran's missile capabilities and warned that if Iran is attacked, the ensuing war "will reach Europe." Conservative commentator Ali Qolhaki echoed that view, writing on X that the threat to expand Iran's targets beyond the region likely meant Europe -- namely countries such as Great Britain, Italy, Greece, and Germany who host US armed forces and are part of Washington's global military deployment and logistical support network -- was now in Iran's crosshairs. Iranian media, meanwhile, have framed the statement as a sign that Tehran's policy on the range of its missiles may be shifting. For years, Iran has maintained a 2,000-kilometer limit on the range of its missiles, a cap that former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said he had imposed despite objections from military figures. Embed share Iran's Next Hormuz 'Weapon' Could Hit Google, Meta, and Streaming Services Globally by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:36 0:00 Some outlets now suggest the younger Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since the February 28 strikes that killed his father, is lifting that cap. The semiofficial ISNA news agency said the statement pointed to a redefinition of how far the armed forces are prepared to strike and could be a sign of change in the strategic considerations governing Iran's missile policy. The Young Journalists Club, which is affiliated with state broadcaster IRIB, took it another step. It said Iran's target list had been updated and that its deterrence now extended "beyond the region." The outlet noted that the United States has at least 128 military bases and facilities in 51 countries, from the Middle East to Europe, Africa, and East Asia, and said "the aggressors' bases anywhere in the world" were now on the armed forces' target list. "Tehran is preparing to respond forcefully to an American-Israeli attack, which, according to assessments, is expected to be particularly broad and violent," according to Danny Citrinowicz, a nonresident fellow at the Atlantic Council. "Moreover, it seems the Iranians are seeking to expand their target bank to include assets that were not attacked in previous campaigns, among them communication infrastructures and additional strategic assets in Gulf countries. The implication is that the next campaign, if it erupts, could be far broader, longer, and more grueling than Washington hopes." Not everyone is convinced the rhetoric means a change in policy. The reformist daily Etemad cautioned that calling for longer-range missiles, having the technical capability to build them, and formally deciding to change course are three different things. Map: Iran Launches Missiles Towards Diego Garcia Jeremy Binnie, a Middle East defense analyst with the global intelligence company Janes, offered another reading, saying the reference to geographical restrictions might not be about distance at all. Iran may currently have an agreement with one or more Arab states in the Persian Gulf not to target them, he said, "a restriction that could be lifted." Binnie said Iran has had the ability to extend the range of its missiles beyond 2,000 km "for some time," since range can be increased by reducing warhead weight. The most obvious candidate is the Khorramshahr, unveiled in 2017 and, in Binnie's words, "their most powerful missile." It has been estimated to have a range of 3,000 km when fitted with a small, 750-kilogram re-entry vehicle it has been seen carrying, he said in written comments to RFE/RL. The 2,000-km limit "made some sense," Binnie said, because it allowed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) to strike "pretty much everything it would need to target in the region" without threatening Europe, with the exception of Cyprus and some Greek islands. Reaching Western Europe would require Iran to extend the range of its missiles. The most obvious target beyond that range, he said, would be Diego Garcia, the joint US-British base in the Indian Ocean nearly 4,000 km from Iranian territory. Britain said Iran attempted but failed to hit the base on March 20, though at least one Iranian official denied such an attempt was made. Is Europe In Iran's Crosshairs? https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-ukraine-w.body: News Moscow Reports Drone Attack On Nizhny Novgorod As Russian Strikes Cut Power In Ukraine By RFE/RL November 01, 2026 12:20 CET Updated November 01, 2026 22:18 CET Moscow Reports Drone Attack On Nizhny Novgorod As Russian Strikes Cut Power In Ukraine Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Video footage from Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region shared on November 1 appears to show the LukOil refinery in flames following a "massive drone attack." Moscow and Kyiv traded strikes on November 1, with dozens of drones reportedly destroyed over Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region and energy infrastructure hit in four Ukrainian regions, leaving hundreds of thousands without power. The governor of Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, Gleb Nikitin, said that an "industrial enterprise" in the Kstovo district had been struck by a "massive drone attack" overnight, causing "significant damage." He added that more than 100 drones were destroyed in the attack, with no casualties reported so far. Ukrainian media reports suggested the strike had hit the LukOil refinery in Kstovo as well as the combined heat and power plant in Novogorkovskaya. RFE/RL could not independently verify the information. SEE ALSO: Rubio Casts Doubts On Quick Deal To End War In Ukraine, Defends Russian Contacts The development came less than 24 hours after the Ukrainian military said it targeted the Russian state-owned Kombinat Kamensky chemical and defense enterprise in Russia's Rostov region with drones and Neptune coastal missile systems. Bordering Ukraine, the region is a strategically important industrial and logistics hub in southwestern Russia. Last month, Reuters reported that Russia had nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones there in just six weeks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that the October 31 attack on the Rostov region had caused tens of millions of dollars' worth of damage, as Kyiv seeks to curb Moscow's war efforts with what it calls "long-range sanctions," referring to its strikes inside Russia. With the Kremlin showing no interest in compromising to end the war while continuing to pound Ukraine with devastating strikes, the country's military has increasingly responded by targeting energy and military sites deep inside Russia. On November 1, Zelenskyy said Russia attacked energy infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, leaving hundreds of thousands without power as cold weather sets in accross the Eastern Europe. "Just this night, our energy sector in four regions was under Russian attacks: Dnipro, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytsky. These are substations, transformers, and power lines that provide electricity to our people's homes," he wrote on Telegram. SEE ALSO: 'Life On Every Street': Ukrainians In Kherson Welcome Cease-Fire In Nearby Oleshky "Repair crews are working everywhere. As of now, hundreds of thousands of families remain without electricity," Zelenskyy said, adding that this week along Russia has launched 1,940 strike drones, over 1,580 glide bombs, and 44 missiles of various types over Ukraine, 36 of which are ballistic. "The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic interceptors," he added. The Ukrainian military said Russian forces attacked the country with 433 drones just on November 1 and that the drones were fired from Oryol and Shatalovo in Russia, as well as the Russian-occupied region of Donetsk. Last Day Of Oleshky Cease-Fire The evacuation of residents from the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been completed as Moscow and Kyiv continued a localized cease-fire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump on November 1. Trapped in the largely ruined city, which was surrounded by land mines and cut off from the outside world, Oleshky residents had endured extreme conditions for months, with little to no access to food, drinking water, medicine, or electricity. On October 30, dozens of buses carrying civilians left the war-torn area for the first time in more than four years without incident, with people choosing whether to travel to Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory. Melania Trump said on November 1 that "the ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack." "Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace," she wrote on X . Zelenskyy, thanking the United States and Melania Trump for their mediation, said residents who wished to travel to Ukraine had crossed into the country on October 31. "Until we got on the buses, we were still afraid," Oleshky evacuee Liubov told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service. "We were so worried and nervous. Before that, we couldn't sleep at night, wondering how this would go." Embed share Tears Of Joy As Ukrainians Evacuated From Russian-Occupied Oleshky Reunite With Family by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:14 0:00 Direct link 240p | 3.2MB 360p | 4.4MB 480p | 6.6MB 720p | 11.0MB 1080p | 18.8MB Just before midnight on November 1, Ukrainian Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the truce had concluded . "The cease-fire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended," he said. "This was an important stage of joint humanitarian work together with the Russian Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova, coordinated by the first lady of the United States, Melania Trump." While the humanitarian efforts in Oleshky have set a rare precedent for cooperation between Ukrainian and Russian civilian representatives, the Kremlin said the temporary cease-fire there should not be extrapolated to the broader peace settlement process in Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly said it was not seeking a partial easing of the conflict, urging a complete resolution that would include its hard-line demands, including full control over Ukrainian territories that Russian forces have been unable to seize on the battlefield. Zelenskyy, in turn, has been for years calling for a leaders' meeting in response, saying that issues surrounding control of Ukrainian territories have to be discussed at the highest level. As Russian and Ukrainian officials are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi in mid-November amid US-mediated negotiations to end the war, a senior Russian official said that Russian President Vladimir Putin would respond if Zelenskyy wished to speak to him by phone. "I think he will, of course. Putin has never refused to talk," Putin aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted as telling Russian media on November 1. Putin has previously sought to cast doubt on Zelenskyy's legitimacy and has repeatedly said the presidents could only meet when a comprehensive peace deal has been agreed, though he has also suggested he and Zelenskyy could meet in Moscow. The Kremlin knows that the prospect of a meeting in the capital of the country that is attacking Ukraine is unacceptable to Kyiv. Zelenskyy has expressed readiness to meet with Putin in a third country. https://www.omct.org/en/resources/urgent.body: Share New information THA 003 / 0625 / OBS 35.1 Conviction / Sentence / Arbitrary detention / Judicial harassment / Restriction to freedom of expression / Restriction to peaceful assembly Thailand 30 October 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), has received new information and requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Thailand . New information: The Observatory has been informed about the conviction and prison sentence imposed on Mr Arnon Nampa, a prominent pro-democracy activist, human rights lawyer, and recipient of the 2025 Front Line Defenders Award for Human Rights Defenders at Risk and four other pro-democracy activists, Ms Wanwalee “Tee” Thammasattaya , Mr Phongsatorn “Boy” Tancharoen , Mr Promsorn “Fah” Veerathamjaree , and Mr Nawat “Amp” Liangwattana. On 30 October 2026, the Criminal Court convicted the five activists under Article 112 of the Criminal Code (“lèse-majesté”) in connection with their participation in a peaceful pro-democracy demonstration outside the headquarters of the Siam Commercial Bank (SCB) in Bangkok on 25 November 2020. The Court sentenced each of them to four years in prison, which was reduced to two years and eight months each, as the Court considered their testimonies useful. Wanwalee Thammasattaya and Phongsatorn Tancharoen were detained at the Bangkok Remand Prison pending the Court of Appeal’s decision on their bail application. Promsorn Veerathamjaree and Nawat Liangwattana have already been imprisoned at the Thanyaburi District Prison and the Bangkok Remand Prison respectively, as a result of other prior lèse-majesté convictions and prison sentences. Promsorn Veerathamjaree had previously undertaken a hunger strike for more than 60 days to demand his release on bail. Mr Arnon Nampa remains detained at the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been incarcerated since his first lèse-majesté conviction on 26 September 2023. On 25 November 2020, a peaceful pro-democracy demonstration was held outside the headquarters of SCB on Ratchadapisek Road in Bangkok. The rally was organised by the United Front of Thammasat and Demonstration and Free Youth and brought together approximately 2,000 protesters calling for the resignation of then Prime Minister General Prayut Chan-o-cha, constitutional amendments and reform of the monarchy. During the demonstration, Mr Nampa delivered a speech regarding legislation on the Thai monarchy and addressed the management and transfer of royal assets. The Crown Property Bureau, recently renamed the Privy Council Purse, and King Rama X are major shareholders of SCB. The Observatory underscores that Mr Nampa has been convicted 12 times under Article 112 of the Criminal Code (“lèse-majesté”) in connection with social media posts and speeches delivered during peaceful pro-democracy demonstrations between 2020 and 2021. The additional two years and eight months of imprisonment imposed on Arnon Nampa under Article 112 bring his total prison term to 34 years, five months, and 20 days. All convictions and prison sentences are currently under appeal, while numerous bail applications have been consistently denied. Between September 2023 and February 2026, he submitted 93 bail applications and 43 appeals against bail denial orders, all of which were rejected. Promsorn Veerathamjaree will now have to serve a total of 10 years and two months in prison, as a result of three prior lèse-majesté convictions and prison sentences. Nawat Liangwattana will now have to serve a total of eight years and eight months in prison, as a result of two prior lèse-majesté convictions and prison sentences. According to Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, between 24 November 2020 and 6 October 2026, at least 294 people, including numerous human rights defenders and 20 minors, were charged under Article 112 of the Criminal Code. As of 31 July 2026, 12 were detained pending trial or appeal, and 17 others were serving prison sentences. The systematic abuse of Articles 112 and 116 against peaceful critics and protesters reflects a broader pattern of judicial harassment and a shrinking civic space in Thailand. On 30 August 2024, the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD) found Arnon Nampa’s detention to be “arbitrary” and urged the Thai government to release him “immediately” and “accord him an enforceable right to compensation and other reparations”. This opinion was issued in response to a petition filed jointly by the Observatory and Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) on 5 March 2024. The Observatory deeply regrets that, more than two years after the WGAD called for Mr Nampa’s immediate release, the Thai authorities have failed to implement the Working Group’s Opinion and have instead continued to prosecute and sentence him under Article 112. The Observatory recalls that Thailand is a State party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). Articles 9 and 14 of the ICCPR guarantee the rights to liberty and to a fair trial, while Articles 19, 21, and 22 protect the rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, and association. Any restriction must be strictly necessary and proportionate. The imposition of lengthy prison sentences for peaceful criticism of public institutions is incompatible with these obligations. The Observatory considers that the conviction and continued arbitrary detention of Arnon Nampa as well as the convictions and prison sentences imposed on Ms Wanwalee Thammasattaya, Mr Phongsatorn Tancharoen, Mr Promsorn Veerathamjaree, and Mr Nawat Liangwattana, appear to be solely aimed at punishing them for their legitimate human rights activities and the peaceful exercise of their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly, in violation of international human rights law. The Observatory calls on the Thai authorities to immediately and unconditionally release the five activists, as well as to release all other arbitrarily detained human rights defenders in the country, and to put an end to all forms of judicial harassment against them. Action requested: Please write to the authorities of Thailand asking them to: Guarantee in all circumstances the physical integrity and psychological well-being of Arnon Nampa, Wanwalee Thammasattaya, Phongsatorn Tancharoen, Promsorn Veerathamjaree, Nawat Liangwattana, and all other human rights defenders and pro-democracy activists in Thailand; Immediately and unconditionally release Mr Arnon Nampa and all other detained human rights defenders and pro-democracy activists whose detention appears to be solely aimed at punishing them for their legitimate human rights activities, and ensure that the other defendants are not subjected to arbitrary detention; Quash the convictions against Arnon Nampa, Wanwalee Thammasattaya, Phongsatorn Tancharoen, Promsorn Veerathamjaree, and Nawat Liangwattana, and cease all acts of harassment, including at the judicial level, against them and all other human rights defenders and pro-democracy activists in the country; Guarantee in all circumstances the rights to freedom of expression and of peaceful assembly, as enshrined in international human rights law, and particularly in Articles 19 and 21 of the ICCPR, in particular by refraining from using Article 112 of the Criminal Code to target human rights defenders and pro-democracy activists. https://www.azattyq.org/a/33888836.html.body: ЖАҢАЛЫҚТАР Қазақстанда мәслихат сайлауының үгіт-насихат науқаны басталды. 11 мыңға тарта кандидат тіркелген 2 қараша 2026 жыл, 15:16 Қазақстанда мәслихат сайлауының үгіт-насихат науқаны басталды. 11 мыңға тарта кандидат тіркелген Бөлісу Сілтемесін көшіру Facebook X (Twitter) WhatsApp Email Бөлісу Бөлісу Сілтемесін көшіру Facebook X (Twitter) WhatsApp Email Бөлісу PDF VPN-сіз оқу Сайт бұғатталып тұрса да, материалды осы сілтемемен кіріп оқуға болады Google-да басымдық бер Орталық сайлау комиссиясының мәслихат сайлауы жөніндегі отырысы. Комиссия мәліметінше, 29 қарашада өтетін сайлауға барлығы 10 971 кандидат тіркелген. Оның ішінде партиялық тізім бойынша, 1219 адам, бір мандатты округ бойынша 9752 адам бар. Елдің 20 өңірінде өтетін жергілікті сайлауда түрлі деңгейдегі мәслихат депутаттарына дауыс беріледі. Бір мандатты сайлау округтерінің саны – 3113. Партиялық тізімдегі әйелдер мен жастардың үлесі – 43,2 пайыз. Бір мандатқа орта есеппен 3 адам таласпақ. Бюллетеньде "бәріне қарсымын" деген таңдау болады. Орталық сайлау комиссиясы өткізген жеребе бойынша, бюллетеньде партиялар мынадай тәртіппен жазылады: 1. "Ауыл" партиясы; 2. "Жалпыұлттық социал-демократиялық партия"; 3. "Қазақстанның Халық партиясы"; 4. "Respublica" партиясы; 5. "Ақ жол" Қазақстанның демократиялық партиясы; 6. Қазақстанның "Байтақ" жасылдар партиясы; 7. "Әділет" партиясы.
